newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. balloonist ends round-the-world bid in India.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist ends round-the-world bid in India.

text.p: A U.S. adventurer fell short on Monday of his dream to become the first person to fly nonstop around the world in a balloon but broke a 16-year-old endurance record before landing safely in northern India.

Steve Fossett touched down at 1:10 p.m. (0740 GMT) about 120 km (75 miles) northwest of Varanasi in remote Prithviganj town, about halfway around the world from his U.S. starting point, air traffic control officials in the Indian capital said.
"He is safe," Delhi air traffic control chief J.S. Ahuja told Reuters.
Fossett was forced to abandon his quest for one of manned flight's oldest goals after his shimmering "Solo Spirit" ran short of fuel.
The commodity broker-turned-adventurer had to take a detour around Libya when Tripoli denied him the right to fly over that North African country on Friday.
Libya later granted permission but not before Fossett had headed south, burning extra fuel.
Fossett began his flight late last Monday night in St Louis, Missouri.
Shortly before landing, he broke the endurance record of six days, 16 minutes for a manned balloon flight, set in 1981 by Americans Ben Abruzzo and Troy Bradley.
On Friday, Fossett broke his own record for balloon distance travel when he passed 8,747 km (5,435 miles) over Algeria. He set the earlier mark on a flight from South Korea to Canada.

The 52-year-old Colorado-based Fossett's support team in Chicago told BBC television he had enough fuel to carry on well beyond India, probably as far as the Pacific, but that would have made for a much more dangerous landing.
Fossett's project manager, Bo Kemper, said he believed the adventurer would make another bid for the around-the-world record next year.
A spokesman for the U.S. embassy in New Delhi said Fossett had been accompanied by a plane carrying support team members, and he might come to the Indian capital.
For much of Monday morning, Fossett circled over Varanasi, one of the Hindu religion's holiest cities, known for its bathing "ghats", or steps, that descend into the Ganges River.
He finally set down in Prithviganj, a small town between Varanasi and Lucknow cities in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh, some 600 km (360 miles) southeast of New Delhi, authorities said.
Government officials were rushing to the remote spot.
On Sunday, Fossett battled fatigue, cold and thunderstorms in the final stages of his journey.
His 150-ft (45-metre) double-skinned balloon travelled in excess of 10,000 miles (16,000 km), riding swift winter jet streams in the Northern Hemisphere before he brought it down.
